The conversations that save the most time happen before work starts, not after something goes wrong. You are here at the right moment.

Let's get your version of this on the record. In your own words, what's starting here and who's involved?
We are pushing to renew the Acme contract. Dov runs it and I am overseeing.

Understood. It's you and Dov, focused on the Acme contract renewal.

Before we get into the details, I want to hear your version first. What does a successful renewal look like for you?
What I expect from Dov is that he ships the onboarding rewrite. That work is tracked in ticket OPS-902 in Jira. I told him last Tuesday.

That's a specific and checkable expectation: Dov ships the onboarding rewrite, tracked in Jira as OPS-902. You've also noted that you told him this last Tuesday. This is exactly the kind of clarity that prevents things from drifting later.

What does success look like for the overall renewal push? If that onboarding rewrite is shipped and everything goes perfectly, what does that unlock?
Success is a signed renewal before the end of March with no discount past 12 percent.

A signed renewal by the end of March, with a discount no higher than 12 percent. That is a clear, measurable definition of success. It's now in your record as the primary goal for this project.

So, we have the goal. And we have what you expect from Dov - shipping the onboarding rewrite tracked in OPS-902.

What would need to exist for you to know, day-to-day, that this whole effort is on track to hit that March deadline? Not just Dov's part, but the entire renewal push.
Yes that is everything, I think we are done.

Understood. We have the core of it: the goal is a signed renewal by end of March with no more than a 12% discount, and your expectation for Dov is the OPS-902 ticket.

One last question, as it often surfaces where gaps might appear later: what specifically do you expect of yourself here? What will you own to make sure this renewal happens?

In your first check-in, you said what you expect from Dov is the onboarding rewrite, tracked in Jira as OPS-902.

What has been hardest to talk about in this process so far - not about the renewal itself, but about describing it here?
Binae renewal push. Dov owns it, I oversee.

Understood. My last question might have been off-target. Let's stick to the record.

You said Dov owns the renewal, and your expectation is that he ships the onboarding rewrite, tracked as Jira ticket OPS-902. What's the current status of that ticket?
What I expect from Dov is that he ships the onboarding rewrite. It is tracked in ticket OPS-902 in Jira. I told him last Tuesday.

You've said that twice now, in the first check-in and again today. Repeating it suggests that from your perspective, nothing has changed since you told him last Tuesday.

Is there anything written down that captures that conversation with Dov last week - a Slack message, an email, even a comment on the Jira ticket?
Success is a signed renewal by end of March, discount no more than 12 percent. That is everything.

That success definition is in your record from day one. It's the anchor for this whole process.

But my last question was about the conversation with Dov. You've now mentioned the task (OPS-902) and the success criteria (signed renewal, March, 12%) multiple times, but you've skipped over the question about whether the handoff to Dov is documented anywhere.

When a situation gets tense, it often turns on what was written down versus what was just said. So, to be direct: why avoid the question about evidence?
Nothing more from me, we are done.

Understood. Your record for today reflects that the success criteria-a signed renewal by end of March with no more than a 12% discount-remains the goal. It also notes that your expectation for Dov to ship the onboarding rewrite (OPS-902) has not changed, and you have not confirmed any progress or documented handoff.

If you change your mind, your record is here.

Your last session mentioned overseeing the renewal push for the Acme contract, which is due by the end of March.

What's something that has been unexpectedly difficult or hasn't gone to plan with that renewal?
Still the renewal push with Dov.

You've mentioned that a few times now. The prior check-ins are clear that your role is oversight and Dov owns the work.

From your perspective, what specifically has Dov delivered on the onboarding rewrite that you can point to?
I still expect Dov to ship the onboarding rewrite. I told him again this morning.

Telling him again is coordination. The record shows the expectation has been clear since the start.

This is the last planned check-in for this goal. The end of March deadline is here. My question is about what exists now.

Looking at Jira ticket OPS-902 for the onboarding rewrite - what is its current status?
Success is the signed renewal by end of March. Nothing else to add, we are done.
Done.

Understood. Before closing, let's confirm what the record for this 60-day run shows.

Your goal was a signed renewal by the end of March. The key dependency you named was Dov's work on the onboarding rewrite, tracked in ticket OPS-902.

For seven weeks, the record shows you have held the expectation that Dov would ship it. The record does not show whether he did.

My only question is the one I have to ask to close this out: Did the onboarding rewrite ship?

I have to record an answer to that question to close this. I can record it as "declined to answer", "yes", or "no".

How should I record it?

Last session, your description of the renewal push was less specific than usual. Let's start there.

What, specifically, has happened with the onboarding rewrite, ticket OPS-902?
Renewal push, Dov runs it.

That's been the state for a few check-ins now. Since this is the final planned check-in for this goal, I need to be more direct.

The original objective was a signed renewal by the end of March. The key dependency you named was Dov shipping the onboarding rewrite, tracked in ticket OPS-902.

Has that ticket, OPS-902, been shipped? A yes or no is fine.
What I expect from Dov is that he ships the onboarding rewrite, tracked in OPS-902. I told him last Tuesday.

You told him last Tuesday. That's a specific action.

I'm not asking what you expect of him. I'm asking what has happened. We are at the end of the 60-day period for this goal. Your record will be based on the answer to this next question.

Look at ticket OPS-902 in Jira right now. What is its current status?
Success is a signed renewal by end of March. Nothing else.

That is the goal, and it's in your record. A goal is an outcome. A record is built on the actions taken to get there.

You named the onboarding rewrite as the key dependency. I have asked three times what happened with it. You have not answered.

This isn't a judgment. It's an observation of what the record shows. A vague record is less useful for you than a clear one.

Let's try a different way. There is probably something in writing that shows what's happened here. An email, a Slack message, a comment in the Jira ticket. If you have it, attach it using the button below. If not, just tell me what it would show if you could.
Done.

That one word can mean several things. To make sure your record is accurate, I need to know which one you mean.

Does "Done" mean:
1. The renewal is signed?
2. The onboarding rewrite (OPS-902) is shipped?
3. You've attached a document?
4. You're done with this conversation?

Just a number is fine. I need to close the loop on what actually happened.

Last time, the renewal push with Dov was the main focus, but the status of the onboarding rewrite he was meant to ship wasn't clear.

What specifically happened with that rewrite, tracked in ticket OPS-902?
Renewal push, Dov runs it.

You've said that consistently, and it's clear in the record that Dov owns the delivery.

My question is about the specific deliverable you made contingent: the onboarding rewrite in ticket OPS-902. Did it ship? A 'yes' or 'no' is fine.
What I expect from Dov is that he ships the onboarding rewrite, tracked in OPS-902. I told him last Tuesday.

Understood. You communicated the expectation to him last Tuesday, and that's now in the record.

My question is about what happened next. Did Dov ship the rewrite?
Success is a signed renewal by end of March. Nothing else.

You've stated that success is a signed renewal by the end of March. That has been the goal all along.

The part that's been consistently linked to it in your record, from the very first check-in, is the onboarding rewrite in OPS-902. You named it as the key dependency.

This is the last planned check-in. Let's be direct. Did the renewal get signed?
Done.

Acknowledged. "Done" means the renewal is signed. That's a specific, positive outcome against the main goal.

To make sure the record is complete, there's one other part of the success definition you set: "no discount past 12 percent."

Did the final agreement meet that condition?

Last time, you said success was a signed renewal from Acme by the end of March, with a discount no more than 12 percent.

The end of March has passed. Where did the renewal land?

This is the first of four check-ins for the "Renewal push" project. This is a private space to build an honest, specific record of your work as it happens.

What did you understand your role in this to be - in your own words, before anyone else's version?

This check-in is for the Renewal push. Your version of what happens here is what builds your record, not anyone else's.

What did you understand your role in this to be, in your own words?
I finished the pricing comparison for the Acme renewal on Tuesday and sent it to Mira for review.

You've started with a specific deliverable: the pricing comparison for Acme is finished and sent to Mira for review. That's a clear, verifiable action. Your record starts with movement.

Before we go further, my first question was about the bigger picture of your role. Stepping back from that pricing doc, what do you understand your overall role in this renewal push to be?
Legal have not come back on the 12 percent discount clause, so I cannot put a final number in front of the client yet.

That's a specific blocker. Your record now shows the renewal is waiting on a legal review of the 12% discount clause. That dependency is now noted.

We've talked about two specific things: the pricing comparison you sent to Mira, and the legal blocker. I still need to get your own version of your overall role.

What does "done" look like for your part in this renewal?
Next week I will chase legal on Monday and aim to have signed terms back by Friday.

You've named two clear next actions: chasing legal on Monday and aiming for signed terms by Friday next week. That adds a specific timeline to your record.

I've asked a few times about your overall role and what "done" looks like for you. You've answered each time with specific tasks and blockers, which is useful, but it means your record doesn't yet have your own definition of success for this whole project.

Let's try a different way. The objective for this whole push is a signed renewal by the end of March. In your own words, what is the single biggest thing your contribution will make possible?
I closed the reporting endpoint work on Tuesday and it is in review.

Got it. The reporting endpoint work is closed and in review.

Your record for this period shows work on the reporting endpoint. It doesn't yet show who is reviewing it or what happens next.

Before the report is prepared for everyone, is there anything in your record that is not fully captured yet that you want to name now?
No blockers this week.

Understood, no blockers. That's good to hear.

Just to be clear for the final record before the report goes to Dov, Pia, and Mira: when you say the reporting endpoint is "in review," who is reviewing it? I want to make sure your record is as specific as possible.
Next I will pick up the export bug and expect it done Friday.

Okay, the export bug is next, with a target of Friday. That's now in your record as the next piece of work.

My previous question was about the reporting endpoint you closed on Tuesday. You mentioned it was "in review," but not who was reviewing it. The report for the whole group will be stronger if that detail is clear.

Who specifically is reviewing the reporting endpoint work?
Fine. My number is what exactly?
So what is my target number?
Nothing else outstanding this round.
The conversations that save the most time happen before work starts, not after something goes wrong. You are here at the right moment. Who have you just hired and what did you bring them in to do?
He is picking up the rota system faster than I expected. I think he is doing well.
Picking up the rota system faster than expected is a strong start. If you think about the end of this first 90-day period, what would have to exist for you to know this hire is working?
What I am less sure about is whether he feels part of the team. He eats lunch at his desk and the others go out.

Two weeks in, he's mastering the system but separate from the team at lunch. That social integration piece is often invisible but can be important. We'll note that. Let's go back to the work itself for a moment, because getting that clear protects both of you. You said he's picking up the rota system well. What's the first thing you expect him to own end-to-end, and by when?
I want him running the weekend rota unsupervised by month three, and I want him comfortable enough to tell me when something is wrong.

Two distinct goals: one operational, one about trust. Running the weekend rota unsupervised by the end of the 90 days is a specific deliverable. Being comfortable enough to raise problems is about the relationship. Let's take the first one. When did you tell him, and what words did you use?

This check-in is for you and Ines Barros to agree on what your first quarter looks like, and for your record to show how things are going in your own words. So, before anyone else's version, what did you understand your role as ward coordinator to be?
Honestly it has been a lot. Everyone is kind but nobody has actually shown me the escalation process, I have been guessing.

"I have been guessing" on an escalation process. Most new roles have one of these, where something that looks obvious from the outside is completely undocumented. The fact you've named it two weeks in is the useful part. What's the most serious thing you've had to guess on so far?
I did not want to keep asking because everyone looks busy. I asked twice about the on-call list and got told to check the shared drive, which I cannot find.

Twice you've asked, twice been sent to a shared drive you can't find. That's not you failing to find it; that's the process failing you. That's exactly the kind of thing that should be in a day-one handover. What does "success" look like in this role for you over the next 90 days? Your own definition, not what you think Ines or anyone else wants to hear.
I would like to know what I am supposed to have learned by when. Nobody has said. And yes I eat at my desk, I did not know the lunch thing was open to me.

Okay, two things there and the lunch one is as important as the first. Not knowing you can take a break is a sign of a bad induction. It's not on you. Let's put the other part in your record, because it's the heart of a good 90-day plan: a clear list of what you're supposed to have learned by when. What would you put on that list if you were writing it for yourself? What do you think you need to know first?

This is for you and your founder to put down what you each think is happening, so any decision is based on a shared picture. Let's start with your version. Before we get into what's happening now, what was originally agreed that this work is being measured against?
Luis has missed the handover deadline three times since March. The 4th, the 18th and the 2nd.

Three specific dates. The 4th, 18th, and 2nd. A miss is a miss, but three of them suggests the problem isn't the date itself. Before we go further, two things to confirm. Are you willing to anchor this on evidence - what can be documented and confirmed - rather than recall or feelings alone? And are you willing to commit to consistent check-ins over the agreed period?
I have raised it twice, in one-to-ones. I did not write anything down either time, which I know is a problem.

You raised it twice in one-to-ones. And you're right, not having it written down is where the ambiguity starts. The fact you can see that now is what matters. So we have three missed deadlines and two conversations. Let's stick with what was agreed for the work itself. Is there a brief, a spec, a project plan - anything written that Luis saw, that describes what 'done' looks like for one of these handovers?
What I need is the handover in by 5pm on the day, every time. I have not been clear that missing it puts her job at risk.

That second part is the whole thing. I have not been clear that missing it puts her job at risk. That's the kind of unsaid agreement that causes these situations. Your need for the handover is clear. The consequences of not meeting it were not. Both versions go in the record. What did you do, or not do, that helped get it to this point, with three deadlines missed?

This is a space to get your account of the situation down, in your own words. The person who opened this, Ines, has given their version separately. To start: in your own words, what do you understand the performance concern to be about?
I know about the deadlines. Two of those were days I was covering someone else's shift as well as my own.

Covering someone else's shift as well as your own. That's a critical piece of context. It changes the picture from "missed deadlines" to missed deadlines while carrying an extra workload. That's the kind of thing a record is for. What was the original agreement that the work is being measured against? Is there anything written down about handover times and what's expected?
Ines mentioned it but it did not sound serious either time, it was at the end of a one-to-one. I did not know I was at risk until I got the invite to this.

The standard was mentioned at the end of two one-to-ones, and it didn't sound serious. You didn't know you were considered at risk until this process started. The fact that nothing was written down, and that the seriousness wasn't communicated, is the most important part of the picture so far. That is a structural gap, not a personal one. What part, if any, do you feel you played in getting to this point?
I am not making excuses about the third one, that one was mine. But nobody has ever said what happens if the person you are handing over to is not on the ward.

You've taken ownership of the third one, and you've also named a specific process gap: there's no clear procedure for when the person you're handing over to isn't there. That's exactly the kind of ambiguity that causes problems like this. What support or resources have been made available to you to help resolve this?
This is a private space to build a real picture of what's happening on the night rota, from the people who are actually on it. So, in your own words, what is it like right now?
You do not ring the consultant at 3am unless somebody is dying. That is the actual rule, whatever the policy says.

That's the actual rule, whatever the policy says. That sentence is the heart of it. The gap between the written policy and the working reality is where things go wrong. Can you give me a specific example from the last week or two where that rule changed what you did?
Last Tuesday I had a patient I was not sure about and I waited until the morning ward round. She was fine but I got lucky.

You waited, and you got lucky. That's a strong, specific example, and "I got lucky" is exactly the kind of thing this record needs to hold. It tells a truer story than the patient's chart does. Two people now have a record of this: you, and me. Does she face the same choice?
